extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetics/literature
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance on how the language and diction appropriate to metrical poetry differ from prose and rustic speech, and the consequences of metre for choice of words, figures, repetition, and subject-matter. Drawn from a theoretical literary-criticism treatment of Wordsworth's practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of metrical composition differs essentially from prose
rubrics_metrics.description: "Between the language of prose and that of metrical composition, there neither is, nor can be, any essential difference" (Wordsworth's assertion) is contested; the true question is whether modes of expression, construction, and order of sentences fit a serious prose composition but would be disproportionate and heterogeneous in metrical poetry, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic contends that such unfitness "frequently will and ought to exist." One must examine origin and effects of metre: metre springs from a balance of mind controlling passion and thus imposes formal constraints and expectations on diction, figures, sentence-order, and frequency of ornamental language. Examples and comparisons (Gray's sonnet, Lyrical Ballads stanzas) are used to show where prose-like lines may occur in poetry but do not prove identity of the styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre originates from a union of passion and volition and so demands language of excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: "The elements of metre owe their existence to a state of increased excitement... as the metre itself should be accompanied by the general language of excitement... traces of present volition should throughout the metrical language be proportionably discernible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two conditions flow from this origin: (1) metre should accompany language of excitement (vivacity, picturesque diction); (2) metrical diction should show marks of deliberate volition (art applied to passion). The union produces a higher frequency of picturesque and vivifying language than would be natural elsewhere; the poet and reader share an understood compact that entitles the former to supply pleasurable excitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre's effects require correspondent matter — avoid empty ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: "As far as metre acts in and for itself, it tends to increase the vivacity and susceptibility both of the general feelings and of the attention... Where, therefore, correspondent food and appropriate matter are not provided for the attention and feelings thus roused, there must needs be a disappointment felt."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because metre arouses attention by continual surprise and quick reciprocations, the subject-matter must sustain that excitement; otherwise the reader experiences disappointment (analogy: leaping in the dark expecting a larger step). Provide appropriate substantive content to match metrical stimulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not naively adopt 'the very language of men' (rustic speech) for poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to "imitate, and, as far as is possible, to adopt the very language of men" (i.e., rustic life) is impracticable and useless: selection implies prior possession of the language; one cannot adopt a class's language merely by using its words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet must adopt not only words but the order in which such words succeed each other. Rustic diction is characterized by greater disjunction, less prospectiveness, and a want of subordinate arrangement; these properties make it unsuitable for most poetry (except drama or professed imitation). Even 'rustic' language, when purified and reconstructed to conform to grammatical rules, will not differ except insofar as the notions to be conveyed differ. Examples: comparing compact poetic stanzas with loose, conversational paraphrases of the same content shows the mismatch; guidance: make necessary omissions and changes rather than wholesale mimicry of provincial speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rustic language tends to convey insulated facts, not the connexions poets need
rubrics_metrics.description: "The rustic... aims almost solely to convey insulated facts... while the educated man seeks chiefly to discover and express those connexions of things... from which some more or less general law is deducible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry (and educated diction) values facts for the way they lead to discovery of underlying laws/relations — diction must serve to reveal connexions and generalization, not merely report isolated particulars. Thus choose diction that can express relations and abstractions, not only narrow empirical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'best part' of human language arises from reflection on mental acts, not mere familiarity with objects
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best part of human language, properly so called, is derived from reflection on the acts of the mind itself. It is formed by a voluntary appropriation of fixed symbols to internal acts, to processes and results of imagination..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words and combinations derived merely from objects familiar to an uneducated rustic cannot be justly said to form the best part of language. Poetic diction should draw on terms capable of expressing mental operations and imaginative processes. Examples include missionary difficulties where languages lack words for moral/intellectual processes; historically many scholarly phrases passed into popular speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition is a high poetic beauty when rooted in genuine passion, not a mechanical filler
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is indeed very possible to adopt in a poem the unmeaning repetitions, habitual phrases... which an unfurnished or confused understanding interposes... But what assistance to the poet, or ornament to the poem, these can supply, I am at a loss to conjecture. Nothing assuredly can differ... more widely from the apparent tautologies of intense and turbulent feeling."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (a) passionate, intense repetitions (e.g., Biblical Deborah: "At her feet he bowed, he fell..."), which are 'a beauty of the highest kind', and (b) mechanical, vacant repetitions used as fillers by an unfurnished mind, which are anti-patterns. Use repetition only when it expresses sustained, genuine feeling or structural emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: One cannot prove poetic/prose identity by isolated lines that read as prose
rubrics_metrics.description: The occurrence of sentences or passages in poetry that could equally appear in good prose does not prove an essential identity between the two kinds of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic argues that the burden of proof lies with the opponent: it's insufficient to cite isolated prose-like lines (e.g., parts of Gray's sonnet) because the real issue is whether there exist modes of expression and arrangements proper to one and improper to the other. Evaluate whole constructions and contextual functions, not isolated lines or words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction requires an organized prospectiveness of thought (ordering of parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneducated men's order of words is "distinguished... by the greater disjunction and separation in the component parts of that... which they wish to communicate. There is a want of that prospectiveness of mind, that surview, which enables a man to foresee the whole of what he is to convey... and by this means so to subordinate and arrange the different parts according to their relative importance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic (and serious prose) diction benefits from an ability to foresee, subordinate, and organize material so as to present an organized whole; avoid the scattered, episodic ordering characteristic of rustic or unreflective speech unless the poem's form deliberately requires it (e.g., authentic dramatic imitation).
